Each on-premises location advertises the same IP prefixes to AWS, and there is connectivity between on-premises locations.\\\\n\\\\nAdvertising the same summary IP prefix from multiple on-premises locations to AWS creates an \u201canycast\u201d routing setup. The connectivity between on-premises locations is important in this routing scenario, as it ensures traffic can be routed from AWS to on-premises destinations using the nearest AWS Direct Connect Point of Presence (POP). When needed, traffic can traverse the on-premises backbone to reach the final destination.\\\\n\\\\nWe introduce an additional AWS Direct Connect gateway to control how traffic flows from AWS to on premises:\\\\n\\\\n* We advertise 10.0.0.0/8 \u2013 IPv4 and 2001:db8::/32 \u2013 IPv6 from both on-premises locations on all four Transit VIFs. No other more specific routes are advertised from on premises to AWS.\\\\n* We associate VIFs in each AWS Direct Connect POP to a separate Direct Connect gateway \u2013 VIF-1 and VIF-2 are associated with Direct Connect gateway A, while VIF-3 and VIF-4 are associated with Direct Connect gateway B.\\\\n* We configure BGP local preference communities on routes from on premises to ensure the Direct Connect gateways choose primary/backup VIFs. You can also load balance traffic across both VIFs in an AWS Direct Connect POP by setting identical BGP attributes.\\\\n\\\\nWe call these behavior-based Direct Connect gateways because they accommodate a specific routing configuration for traffic from AWS to on premises. You can define your own desired behavior for each Region through a dedicated behavior-based Direct Connect gateway.\\\\n\\\\nThe setup for this scenario is shown in the following diagram (Figure 9):\\\\n\\\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/5b384ce32d8cdef02bc3a139d4cac0a22bb029e8/2024/03/29/Figure9-1-scaled.jpg)\\\\n\\\\nFigure 9: Scenario 3 \u2013 Multi-Region AWS Cloud WAN setup with a transit gateway on each Region, two Direct Connect gateways, multiple AWS Direct Connect connections associated with two Regions and a backbone network connecting the colocation facilities\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/advanced-hybrid-routing-scenarios-with-aws-cloud-wan-and-aws-direct-connect/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Traffic Segmentation Options in AWS Direct Connect\",\"context\":\"## Segment Your Traffic over AWS Direct Connect by Using Several Private VIFs in the VPC or Direct Connect Gateway diagram\\\\n\\\\nPrivate virtual interfaces (VIFs) are used to access Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) using private IP addresses.\\\\nEach VIF is configured with an unique virtual local area network (VLAN) tag, which\\\\nmeans you can segment your traffic by using one VIF per virtual routing and\\\\nforwarding (VRF) you have in your data center. Take into account the limits in\\\\nthe number of VIFs, depending the type of Direct Connect connection you have. You can\\\\nhave 50 private or public VIFs with a dedicated connection, and one private\\\\nor public VIF with a hosted connection. In addition, you can have 30 private\\\\nVIFs associated to the same Direct Connect gateway. You can check the quotas in the\\\\nDirect Connect user guide.\\\\n\\\\n1. Traffic initiated from an instance in Spoke VPC A and destined for the\\\\n corporate data center server (in VRF A) is routed to the virtual private\\\\n gateway according to the Spoke VPC A route table.\\\\n2. The virtual private gateway is associated with the Direct Connect\\\\n gateway, which uses a private VIF (VLAN) to connect to the corporate data center. To achieve\\\\n segmentation, use several private VIFs. The on-premises router must be configured to\\\\n use a different VIF (VLAN) connection per VRF configured.\\\\n3. The on-premises router forwards the traffic from private VIF A to\\\\n VRF A and the destination server.\\\\n4. Traffic from the corporate data center\u2019s VRF B destined for Spoke VPC B\\\\n is first sent to the customer gateway located in the data center.\\\\n5. The customer gateway uses private VIF B \u2013 over the Direct Connect link \u2013 to\\\\n send the traffic to the virtual private gateway in VPC B.\\\\n6. Traffic is forwarded to the destination according to the Spoke VPC B\\\\n route table\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/reference-architecture-diagrams/latest/electronics-hpc/traffic-segmentation-aws-direct-connect.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"AWS Direct Connect Integration with VMware Cloud on AWS | AWS Partner Network (APN) Blog\",\"context\":\"### Private VIF\\\\n\\\\nWhen running critical workloads, in order to have the end-to-end resiliency from on-premises to your SDDC with a Private VIF, you must configure a Private VIF across a minimum of two AWS Direct Connect connections.\\\\n\\\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/77de68daecd823babbb58edb1c8e14d7106e83bb/2021/04/30/VMC-Direct-Connect-9.jpg)\\\\n\\\\n*Figure 9 \u2013 Private VIF resiliency for AWS Direct Connect with VMware Cloud on AWS.*\\\\n\\\\nCustomers can configure two Private VIFs across two different AWS Direct Connect connections in two different locations that terminates on the VGW for the respective VMware Cloud on AWS SDDC.\\\\n\\\\nTo achieve route resiliency for this architecture, you need to use BGP for route management across each of the Private VIFs. You have two options on how to configure BGP to support this architecture:\\\\n\\\\n* **Active/Active:** This is the default configuration for AWS Direct Connect. In this case, the service uses BGP multipath to load balance network traffic across the Private VIFs. If there are two connections and one fails, the traffic will be routed across the other connection.\\\\n\\\\n .\\\\n* **Active/Passive:** With this configuration, one connection is active and handles all the traffic, while the other one is on standby. In case of an outage and the main link fails, the traffic is routed to the standby link that becomes active. AS-Path prepending algorithm and Local preferences are the BGP algorithms and attributes that helps you to achieve that.\\\\n\\\\n .\\\\n\\\\n With AS-Path prepending, you influence the path for the routes advertised over AWS Direct Connect. If you want one of your connections to be passive, you must ensure your on-premises router advertise a longer AS-Path for that connection.\\\\n\\\\n .\\\\n\\\\n In that case, the traffic from the SDDC to the on-premises will chose the active connection, the one with a shorter AS-Path length and lowest Autonomous System number that it needs to go through until the destination.\\\\n\\\\n .\\\\n\\\\n If the AWS Direct Connect locations are different, you also need to use Local Preference \u2013 BGP communities. {"id": "901e81e0-0ee7-4aeb-ae80-99576102415f", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Short answer: **not directly through a basic private VIF setup, but yes with the right design.**

By default, a private VIF just connects your on-premises router to a VGW/Direct Connect gateway, which routes into a VPC. AWS doesn't natively bridge two separate private VIFs to each other — the Direct Connect gateway's job is to get traffic *into* VPCs, not to relay between two on-prem sites.

To get site-to-site connectivity through AWS, you need to introduce something in the middle that can do the routing/relaying between the two VIFs:

- **Transit VIF + Transit Gateway**: Terminate each site on its own transit VIF, attach both to the same Transit Gateway, and let the TGW route table pass traffic between them. This is the standard way to connect multiple on-prem sites to each other via AWS.
- **Direct Connect gateway + VPN/Cloud WAN**: Associate both VIFs with Direct Connect gateways that feed into a hub (Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN core network), which handles the inter-site routing.
- **SiteLink**: If both Direct Connect locations support it, SiteLink lets you route traffic directly between Direct Connect points of presence without transiting a Region at all — useful if you just want site-to-site connectivity without needing it to touch a VPC.

So the pattern that doesn't work: two private VIFs terminating independently on VGWs with no shared hub — AWS won't relay between them. The pattern that does: route both VIFs (as transit VIFs, or via Direct Connect gateway) into a common Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN core, or use SiteLink.

Want me to check your account's current Direct Connect / Transit Gateway setup to see which of these would fit your topology?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
